name: Nora Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a relief milker and general hand at Marsh Farm, outside Fenwick, about two hundred and twenty Holstein cows. I'm in the parlour by half past four for morning milking, then it's scraping out the cubicles, feeding the calves, and back for afternoon milking at three. Owen Marsh runs the place with his son, and I'm the newest one there, three years in, so I get the jobs nobody else wants.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you come to dairy at fifty-five?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The canning factory on Mill Street shut, the one I'd worked at for twenty-eight years, peeling and packing beans mostly. I was the union rep on our line for the last ten. Owen's wife knew me from the factory and said they were short a milker, and I thought, well, I grew up next to cows, how hard can it be. Harder than I thought, is the answer. I still can't spot a cow with mastitis, that's an udder infection, as fast as the young lad does.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the cows, I really do. There's one old girl, number 418, who always waits at the back so she's last into the parlour, and I talk to her like she's a neighbour. What wears me out is my knees on the concrete, and the pay. Henrik, my partner, drove buses until his back went, so we live on my wage and a small bit of his pension, and there's never more than a couple of weeks of money in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, let it stay a tool, and let the people who like computers enjoy it. Most of the lads at the farm already look things up on their phones, so a better search engine doesn't change much in the parlour. Cows still need milking twice a day whatever the computers do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be relieved, because I don't touch any of it. My phone is the old kind with buttons, and my daughter Sigrid sets up anything else for me. If it stays like this, I can keep doing what I'm doing until I'm sixty-six and collect my pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different, really. I'd keep my shifts, keep putting twenty a month into the jar for Christmas, and maybe ask Owen again about the extra Sunday milking. I'd let Sigrid keep doing the online forms like she does now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It feels like being left alone, which is all I want at my age.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the farm next door. Is anything changing there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Brandt's, over the hill, put in milking robots two years ago, the kind where the cow walks in on her own and a machine arm puts the cups on. That's already here, nothing to do with your card. Owen says he can't afford it, and I say thank God for that every morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: So even in the calm picture, there's a robot in the next field. Does that sit in the back of your mind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It does, a bit. When I drive past Brandt's at dawn there's no light on in the parlour, because nobody's in it. I used to know the woman who milked there, Ruth, and she's stacking shelves now.

S0.say: I'd say let it stay a tool, and let the people who like computers enjoy it. Cows still need milking twice a day, whatever the computers do.
S0.think: I'm relieved, because I don't touch any of it and my daughter does the online forms for me. If it stays like this I can keep milking until I reach pension age.
S0.do: Keeps her shifts and her twenty a month Christmas jar. Asks Owen again about the extra Sunday milking and lets her daughter carry on doing the online forms.
S0.feel: Calm, like being left alone, though the robot milkers on the next farm nag at her a little.
S0.quote: When I drive past Brandt's at dawn there's no light on in the parlour, because nobody's in it.
S0.fieldNote: Nora is calm about AI as a tool because she simply doesn't use it. The real unease came from something already real: robot milkers on the neighbouring farm and a former milker now stacking shelves. The dark parlour at dawn is an image she clearly carries with her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the second one. Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's how it's always gone, slowly, and the bosses use slow change to get away with things. At the factory they never sacked anyone, they just didn't replace people when they retired, and the line got faster for the rest of us. I'd say the union should watch the hiring numbers, not just the sackings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm fifty-eight, so slow is fine for me. Ten years is longer than I've got left in the parlour anyway. What bothers me is that I only got this job because Owen was willing to take on a beginner, and if farms stop doing that, the next Nora doesn't get a chance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and do the job well, and I'd try harder to learn the bits I'm bad at, like spotting lame cows early. I'd ask Owen's son to show me the herd records on the computer, which I've avoided for three years. That's about it, I wouldn't change anything big.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, more for other people than me. It's a slow leak, not a burst pipe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd finally look at the herd records on the computer. What's stopped you so far?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pride, mostly, and fear of looking stupid. Callum is twenty-four and he types so fast, and I stand behind him like a fool. Last month he said Gran, no, I mean Nora, and we both laughed, but it stung.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think about when you hear 'fewer beginners'?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My grandson Elias, who's sixteen and wants to work with animals. If the farms around Fenwick stop taking beginners, where does he go? There's only three dairy farms left within twenty miles, and there were eleven when I was a girl.

S1.say: I'd say slow change is how bosses get away with things, by not replacing people who leave. The union should watch the hiring numbers, not just the sackings.
S1.think: At fifty-eight, slow is fine for me, because ten years is longer than I've got left in the parlour. What bothers me is that I only got this job because Owen took on a beginner, and the next one might not get that chance.
S1.do: Works on her weak spots like spotting lame cows. Asks Owen's son to show her the herd records on the computer, which she has avoided for three years.
S1.feel: Uneasy, more for others than herself. She calls it a slow leak, not a burst pipe.
S1.quote: Callum is twenty-four and he types so fast, and I stand behind him like a fool.
S1.fieldNote: Her union past shapes how she reads the slow picture: she knows how jobs vanish by not being refilled. The talk of herd records exposed real embarrassment about her age and slowness with computers. Her worry quickly moved to her grandson and the shrinking number of dairy farms nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Third picture. Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need unions in offices, and I'd say it on the doorstep if anyone asked. Office people always thought unions were for factory types like us. Well, now they'll find out what it's like to be told your job's gone by a letter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Just between us, part of me thinks it's not my fight, because there's no office at Marsh Farm except Owen's kitchen table. But Sigrid does the payroll for the council in town. If her job goes, she can't help me with my forms and she can't help her own kids either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ring Sigrid that week and ask straight out how safe her job is. I'd go to the union branch meeting in Fenwick, the one I stopped going to after the factory closed, and offer to help office people organise. And I'd stop the twenty a month into the Christmas jar in case Sigrid needs it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious for my daughter, and a bit angry. Angry is easier than scared, so I'd lean on angry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually say to Sigrid on that phone call?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, love, join the union tomorrow, not when the letter comes. And she'd say Mum, it's not the factory. And I'd say that's what we all said.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You stopped going to the branch meetings. Why would this get you back?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'd have something to give. At the factory I knew how to stand in front of a manager and not shake. Office people don't know that yet, and I do.

S2.say: I'd say this is why offices need unions, and office workers will now learn what it's like to lose a job by letter. I'd say it to anyone who asked.
S2.think: It isn't really my fight, because there's no office on the farm. But Sigrid does council payroll, and if her job goes, she can't help me or her own kids.
S2.do: Rings her daughter that week and tells her to join the union. Goes back to the Fenwick union branch to help office workers organise, and stops her Christmas savings in case her daughter needs money.
S2.feel: Anxious for her daughter and angry on her behalf. She chooses anger because it's easier than fear.
S2.quote: Angry is easier than scared, so I'd lean on angry.
S2.fieldNote: Her old union skills came back to life here: she sees herself as someone who can teach office workers how to stand up. Her own job isn't threatened, but her daughter is the family's link to forms and computers, so the risk travels back to Nora. She was honest that anger is a way of managing fear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Fourth picture. Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the gains should go to everyone, through taxes and public services, not to whoever owns the computers. If house prices are booming while people are being sacked, that's theft with paperwork. I'd say that at the farm, at the pub, anywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it leaves people like me exactly where we were, and that's the trouble. We don't own shares and we rent our cottage from the Marsh family. If house prices boom, Owen might sell the cottage to some city person, and Henrik and I would be out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Owen, straight, whether he'd ever sell the cottage, and get him to put our tenancy in writing, which we've never done in nine years. I'd sign every petition going for a tax on the big winners. And I'd keep milking, because the cows don't care about the stock market.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, with a lump in my throat about the cottage. The job feels safe for once, but the roof doesn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've never had the tenancy in writing. Why not?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because Owen's a handshake man and I'm a handshake woman. It felt rude to ask for paper. But when house prices go mad, handshakes get forgotten, I've seen it with Ruth's family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Physical jobs are mostly untouched in this picture. Does that comfort you at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little. For once the person in wellies is the lucky one. But I'd rather be lucky and poor than watch my daughter be unlucky and poor, so no, not really.

S3.say: I'd say the gains should be shared through taxes and public services, not kept by whoever owns the computers. Booming house prices while people are sacked is theft with paperwork.
S3.think: It leaves people like me where we were, with no shares and a rented cottage. If house prices boom, Owen might sell the cottage and Henrik and I would be out.
S3.do: Asks Owen whether he'd sell the cottage and gets their nine-year tenancy written down for the first time. Signs petitions for a tax on the big winners and keeps milking.
S3.feel: Anxious, with a lump in her throat about the cottage, even though her job feels safe.
S3.quote: If house prices are booming while people are being sacked, that's theft with paperwork.
S3.fieldNote: The surprise was that her fear moved from the job to the roof over her head. Her tied cottage, rented on a handshake, makes a house price boom a direct threat. She admitted physical work being safe is little comfort while her daughter is at risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last picture. Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should have seen it coming when Brandt's parlour went dark, and I'd say it loudly. Farm workers need a union that can sit at the table when the robots come, and laws that say a farm can't just sack people the week the machine arrives. I'd be at every meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm finished. I'm the newest, the slowest and the oldest, and Owen would be daft to keep me over a machine that milks at three in the morning. It doesn't complain about its knees, either. I'd last maybe a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Owen to tell me early, not on the day, so I had time. I'd sign on with the job centre straight away and ask about anything in the care homes, but your card says robots are there too. Henrik and I would sell the second car, which saves us about ninety a month, and I'd ask Sigrid whether we could move into her spare room if the cottage went with the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Sick, really. Not just the money, it's that I'd be useless, and I've never been useless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to cow 418 on your last day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably cry in the parlour like a silly old woman. She'd be first in line for the robot by then, I bet, they learn quick. I'd tell her she was always my favourite, and she'd ignore me, being a cow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you never use AI tools. If the only job was minding the robots, would you try?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try, because I'm not daft and we'd need the money. But I'd be honest with you, I don't think anyone would pick a fifty-eight-year-old with a button phone for that job. They'd pick Callum, and they'd be right to.

S4.say: I'd say we should have seen it coming when the neighbour's parlour went dark. Farm workers need a union at the table and laws that stop sackings the week the machine arrives.
S4.think: I'd be finished, as the newest, slowest and oldest one there. A machine that milks at three in the morning without bad knees would replace me within about a year.
S4.do: Asks Owen for early warning and signs on at the job centre straight away. Sells the second car to save about ninety a month and asks her daughter about moving into her spare room if the cottage goes with the job.
S4.feel: Alarmed and sick, less about the money than about feeling useless for the first time in her life.
S4.quote: I'm the newest, the slowest and the oldest, and Owen would be daft to keep me over a machine that milks at three in the morning.
S4.fieldNote: Her calm in the first pictures was partly because the threat she fears most is already next door. She was clear-eyed that she would be the first to go and wouldn't be chosen to mind the robots. The thought of feeling useless hurt more than the thought of being poor.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The last one, the robots, because it's the only one that touches me and Henrik and the cottage all at once. What would help is a proper notice period, six months, and someone paying for us older ones to bridge to the pension. Not a course on computers, I'm not going to become a programmer at sixty. Just let us land softly.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the cows. Everyone talks about the workers, but a robot parlour runs cows harder, more milkings, and nobody notices when one's just a bit off. I'd want someone to ask who's watching the animals when there's no person in the shed.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: That's a good point. Anything else?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm not against machines. The parlour itself is a machine. I'm against nobody asking us first.

headlineQuote: When I drive past Brandt's at dawn there's no light on in the parlour, because nobody's in it.
portrait: Nora Larsen is 58 and has been a relief milker on a 220-cow dairy farm for three years, after the canning factory where she was a union rep for a decade closed. She lives with her partner Henrik in a cottage rented from her boss on a handshake, with a couple of weeks of money in the bank, and she doesn't use AI at all. She is calm in the first pictures but already haunted by the robot milkers on the next farm, and her worries move from her grandson's chances, to her daughter's office job, to losing the cottage in a house price boom. In the robot picture she expects to be the first one let go and feels it as a loss of usefulness, not just income.
biggestWorry: The robot picture worries her most, because it hits her job, her partner and her tied cottage all at once.
whatWouldHelp: A six-month notice period and money to bridge older workers to their pension, not computer courses. She'd also want someone checking on animal welfare in robot sheds.
